# Facts — eyewitness and process testimony (F-EW)

Cards are sorted by the date in their "When / where" line (year, month, day). Cards with no year there come last, under "Undated". Each card ends with its extraction ID (batch letter + number) so it can be traced to the working notes.

Locators: "PO n" = Ordinary Process 1910–11, witness n; "PA n" = Apostolic Process 1915–17, witness n; numbers in square brackets are folios/pages of the public copy as printed on the Archives du Carmel pages (sources.md W1–W2). Community pages = W3. Local books = L1–L5.

Rights: Carmel web text is facts-only; French quotations are short; every English rendering is ours. Public-domain English (L1–L5) is marked in its cards.

Batches merged:
- A: PO 1 Mère Agnès (Ordinary Process) — complete; addendum topics only partly carded
- B: PA 6 Mère Agnès (Apostolic Process) — PARTIAL (cards to folio ≈[531] of [552]; no addendum, no summary)
- C: PO 3 Marie du Sacré-Cœur + PO 4 Sr Geneviève (Ordinary) — PARTIAL (to f. ≈403r of 415v; no addendum)
- D: PA 7 Marie du Sacré-Cœur + PA 8 Sr Geneviève (Apostolic) — complete
- E: Novices: PO 17/PA 21 Marie de la Trinité, PO 18 Marie-Madeleine, PO 15/PA 18 Marthe, PA 17 Aimée de Jésus — nearly complete; addendum not applied
- F: PO 13/PA 9 Thérèse de Saint-Augustin, PO 14/PA 10 Marie des Anges, PO 16 Isabelle, PO 7/PA 11 Léonie — PARTIAL (PO 16 thin; no addendum)
- G: Family, teachers, priests (Jeanne Guérin, Benedictines, Pichon, Roulland, Dumaine, Valadier, Lemonnier, chaplains) — complete
- H: Cult and miracle witnesses (Taylor, Élie, Auriault, Weber, Madelaine, Grant, etc.) — PARTIAL (PO 33 Bishop Giannattasio not carded)
- I: Community notes préparatoires, témoignages, souvenirs, Gonzague pages, Léonie lecture — nearly complete; no summary
- J: Céline's Conseils et souvenirs; Marie's autobiographical memories — complete
- K: Gonzague biography; Aimée, Saint-Jean-Baptiste, Saint-Vincent de Paul biographies/circulars — PARTIAL
- L: Local public-domain books: De Teil 1913, Dolan 1926, Taylor 1924, Carmel Foundation 1913, Laveille 1928 (deposition quotes) — complete
- N: Gap-fill batch (F-EW-2448 to F-EW-2670, appended by hand at the end of the file, not date-sorted): Bishop Giannattasio (PO 33); end of Mère Agnès's 1915 deposition (PA 6 [531]–[552]); end of Céline's 1910 deposition (PO 4); Mère Isabelle (PO 16); Léonie, Marie des Anges, Pichon re-reads; circulars of Thérèse de Saint-Augustin, Marie-Élisabeth and Marie de l'Eucharistie; Fr Piat's biography of Marie Guérin; four short nun biographies. Also 65 source-line fixes for "circular" cards in the older batches.

Many events have several cards from different witnesses. They were NOT merged, because each speaker must stay separate. Search by date to find parallel accounts. The sort uses the first year in the When line, so a card about a period (e.g. 1888–1897) sits at its start year.


## Dated cards

### F-EW-001 — Parents: birthplaces, trades, standing
- Claim: Louis-Joseph-Aloys-Stanislas Martin was born in Bordeaux on 22 Aug 1823 and was a jeweller (bijoutier). Marie-Zélie Guérin was born at Gandelain, near Alençon, on 23 Nov 1831 and traded in point d'Alençon lace. When Thérèse was born, her father had retired from business and the family was well-off (aisée).
- When / where: 1823–1873, Alençon
- People: Louis Martin; Zélie Martin
- Witness: Mère Agnès (Pauline Martin), daughter; family knowledge
- Source: PO 1, f. 135r, 136r–v, Session 5, 12 Aug 1910
- New to English readers: no
- Confidence: high
- Notes: —
- Extraction ID: A-F145

### F-EW-002 — Gonzague: identity and offices
- Claim: Marie-Adèle-Rosalie Davy de Virville ("Marie Davy de Virville"), born Caen 20 Feb 1834, entered Lisieux Carmel 29 Nov 1860, professed 27 June 1862; sub-prioress 1866–1872; prioress 1874–1883, 1886–1893 (term extended one year in 1892), 1896–1902; bursar (1st depositary) and novice mistress 1883–86 and 1893–96; in 1896 prioress and novice mistress "seconded by Thérèse"; cancer of the tongue spring 1904; died 17 Dec 1904. In all, 6 years sub-prioress and 21 years prioress.
- When / where: 1834–1904, Lisieux
- People: Mère Marie de Gonzague
- Witness: Sr Cécile's chronological table (modern)
- Source: base + mere-marie-de-gonzague/biographie-mere-marie-de-gonzague/, "Survol biographique"
- New to English readers: partial
- Confidence: high — archival dates
- Notes: gives her family name only as "Marie Davy de Virville".
- Extraction ID: K-F01

### F-EW-003 — A priest who confessed his past before the tribunal
- Claim: Weber, born 25 April 1835 at Lorcelette (diocese of Metz), ordained 11 April 1861, left the ministry in 1873. He was twice suspended a divinis around 1873 (absolved 1874). Around 1884 a German civil court convicted him of immorality ("rightly or wrongly") and sentenced him to six years' prison. He then tried the Cistercians at Lérins (nine months, 1899), left for health, and became a resident priest at Saint-Jean-de-Luz.
- When / where: 1835–1911; Lorraine (then German), Lérins, Le Dorat, Saint-Jean-de-Luz
- People: Abbé Claude-Marcel Weber
- Witness: Weber about himself
- Source: PO-19, f. 1127v–1128r, session 69, 22 March 1911
- Original words: « à tort ou à raison j'ai été condamné à un emprisonnement de six années »
- Translation: rightly or wrongly, I was sentenced to six years' imprisonment
- New to English readers: yes
- Confidence: high
- Notes: He said only obedience to the Church brought him, knowing he would have to make these admissions. He presented testimonial letters from the Bishop of Bayonne. Editors: he died 20 October 1915.
- Extraction ID: H-F63

### F-EW-004 — Sr Saint-Vincent de Paul: identity
- Claim: Zoé-Adèle Alaterre, born Cherbourg 13 Aug 1841, daughter of a stonecutter; orphaned at 8 by cholera (1849), raised by the Sisters of St Vincent de Paul in Caen. Lay sister (voile blanc) at Lisieux from 2 Feb 1864, professed 14 Dec 1865. Very small (perhaps under 1.50 m), frail, vomited blood yearly; a fine embroiderer; made and mended the alpargates (rope sandals). Marie des Anges called her a "doctor of the Sorbonne" who could answer any question; Céline: "fine and sly", devoted to the Virgin; she liked to talk. Died 13 April 1905.
- When / where: 1841–1905
- People: Sr Saint-Vincent de Paul
- Witness: P. Gires biography
- Source: `soeur-st-vincent-de-paul/biographie-de-soeur-st-vincent-de-paul/`
- New to English readers: yes
- Confidence: high
- Extraction ID: K-F125

Expelled in 1903, he took refuge with his community at Leffe abbey near Dinant (diocese of Namur), Belgium.

### F-EW-006 — Mère Geneviève's own humiliation story (context)
- Claim: In her final illness Mère Geneviève told Marie des Anges that when the community wanted her as prioress after Mère Élisabeth's death, a letter from Poitiers told Fr Sauvage: "Geneviève has no capacity." He withdrew his trust. She repeated: "Geneviève is capable of nothing."
- When / where: story of 1842; told 1891
- People: Mère Geneviève; Fr Sauvage; Sr Marie des Anges
- Witness: Sr Marie des Anges, heard it
- Source: https://archives.carmeldelisieux.fr/au-carmel-du-temps-de-therese/la-communaute/soeur-marie-des-anges/notes-autobiographiques-de-soeur-marie-des-anges/
- New to English readers: yes
- Confidence: high
- Notes: Background: the "saint" Thérèse admired had been judged incapable.
- Extraction ID: I-F225

### F-EW-007 — Who Fr Élie was
- Claim: Fr Élie (Jérôme-Vincent Lanaro), born Savona 13 December 1845, was a Discalced Carmelite of Lombardy. He was a missionary in India (Mangalore, Quilon) for about 31 years (1867–1898), then secretary to two Carmelite generals in Rome (1898–1906). He never knew Thérèse.
- When / where: 1845–1910
- People: Fr Élie; Fr Bernardin de Sainte-Thérèse and Fr Raynauld-Marie de Saint-Just (generals)
- Witness: Fr Élie about himself; editors' note adds he briefly joined Garibaldi's troops as a youth, knew Bl. Mariam Baouardy in India, became vicar of Mount Carmel in 1915 and died 20 February 1920
- Source: PO-05, f. 434r–434v, session 37, 28 October 1910; intro
- New to English readers: yes
- Confidence: high
- Notes: The editors' intro gives folios 443r–454r; the text itself starts at [434r]. One of the two is a misprint.
- Extraction ID: H-F33

### F-EW-009 — Sr Saint-Jean-Baptiste: identity
- Claim: Marie-Estelle Dupont, born Coulommiers 10 Oct 1847, daughter of a basket-maker; a servant to the Hamel de la Barquerie family, refugee at Lisieux in 1870. Entered 7 Oct 1871 (named for the superior, Jean-Baptiste Delatroëtte); professed 8 May 1873. First linen-keeper in 1893; tall, handsome bearing, fine embroiderer, made flower motifs in hair. Died 27 Oct 1917 after one day's illness, unconscious; Agnès wrote no circular "for several reasons".

### F-EW-010 — Who Fr Flamérion was
- Claim: Anatole-Armand-Marie Flamérion, born Paris (parish of Saint-François-Xavier) 7 October 1851, son of a Paris municipal employee, Jesuit. He taught in a college for 15 years, preached, and from 1900 directed the Villa Manrèse at Clamart, a house of priests' retreats. From 1909 he was official exorcist of Paris, succeeding Fr de Haza, whose "socius" he had been for nine years.
- When / where: 1851–1916; Paris, Clamart
- People: Fr Flamérion SJ; Fr de Haza SJ; Cardinal Amette (who delegated him as exorcist)
- Witness: Flamérion about himself; editors' note
- Source: PO-23, f. 1175v–1177r, session 74, 3 April 1911; PA-20, p. 1097–1098, session 58, 25 August 1916
- New to English readers: yes
- Confidence: high
- Notes: The PO-23 intro says he taught ten years; he says 15. Editors: he died in Paris in 1925. 400 to 500 priests came to Villa Manrèse each year (PO-23, f. 1179v).
- Extraction ID: H-F71

### F-EW-011 — Zélie's locution: "Fais faire du Point d'Alençon"
- Claim: Zélie told Marie that at 20–22 she learned lace at a manufacturer's but left when her virtue was not safe there. On the feast of the Immaculate Conception, making her bed, she heard distinctly "Have Point d'Alençon made". With her sister she started at once, found Paris houses; she signed the first contract because her elder sister was absent — a sign, since the sister later entered the Visitation.
- When / where: c. 1851–53, Alençon
- Witness: Marie — HEARD from Zélie
- Source: MSC, Cahier
- New to English readers: yes
- Confidence: medium — family memory; see M-EW-001
- Extraction ID: J-F177

### F-EW-012 — Family: Zélie's lace business and how it began
- Claim: Zélie's parents had no fortune. Around 20–22 her mother had her learn Point d'Alençon at a manufacturer's; she left because her virtue was not safe there. She then set up her own lace business with her sister (the future Sr Marie-Dosithée), found Paris houses to buy, and signed the first contract herself. Marie remembers Zélie working "ardently" at her lace while the maid took the children out, and scolding Louise's pride in Céline's pretty clothes.
- When / where: c. 1851 onward, Alençon
- People: Zélie; Élise Guérin (Sr Marie-Dosithée)
- Witness: Marie — HEARD from Zélie; SAW the work
- Source: MSC, Cahier
- New to English readers: partial
- Confidence: medium
- Extraction ID: J-F187

### F-EW-013 — Sr Aimée de Jésus: identity
- Claim: Léopoldine-Marie-Céline (circular: Cécile) Féron, born 24 Jan 1851 at Anneville-en-Saire (Cotentin), second of seven children of well-off farmers. As a child she tore off a toenail with a penknife to "test herself for martyrdom", and fought her mother violently until about 11. Left school early to save her parents money. Tried the Charterhouse for three tearful weeks, then entered Lisieux 11 Oct 1871 as a choir nun (she had wished to be a lay sister); professed 8 May 1873 with Sr Saint-Jean-Baptiste. Infirmarian (with Sr Adélaïde, then first infirmarian), later linen room and heavy laundry, carpentry. Died 7 Jan 1930.
- When / where: 1851–1930
- People: Sr Aimée de Jésus du Cœur de Marie
- Witness: circular (Agnès, 17 Jan 1930); biography (P. Gires)
- Source: `sr-aimee-de-jesus/circulaire-sr-aimee-de-jesus/`; `sr-aimee-de-jesus/biographie-sr-aimee-de-jesus/`
- New to English readers: yes
- Confidence: high
- Notes: birth name "Céline" (bio) vs "Cécile" (circular); birth year 1851 (bio) vs 1852 (circular heading).
- Extraction ID: K-F133

### F-EW-016 — The parents' religious practice
- Claim: Both parents went daily to the 5:30 a.m. Mass and received Communion four or five times a week; late in life Louis received daily. Louis belonged to the St Vincent de Paul Conference and to Nocturnal Adoration. Both kept the Lenten fast and abstinence despite Zélie's weak health. Louis kept Sunday strictly and closed his jewellery shop that day at a real financial loss.
- When / where: 1858–1894, Alençon and Lisieux
- People: Louis Martin; Zélie Martin
- Witness: Mère Agnès; SAW

- Claim: Before his marriage, Louis had placed a statue of the Virgin in a garden alley. It was the same statue that later stood in the child's room during the 1883 illness. Zélie had received "very great favours" at its feet.

### F-EW-018 — The Virgin statue's origin: Félicité Baudouin
- Claim: The big Virgin statue (later "of the Smile") was given to Louis before his marriage by Mlle Félicité Baudouin, an old lady devoted to him who paid the first costs of his watchmaking shop. It stood in the Pavillon garden in a leafy bower. Zélie refused to let Marie remove it from her room ("while I live this Virgin will not leave here"). In May Zélie paid a woman to buy big hawthorn branches so the Virgin was lost in flowers. After Zélie's death Marie insisted it come to Lisieux.
- When / where: before 1858 onward; Alençon
- People: Félicité Baudouin
- Witness: Marie
- Source: MSC, Cahier
- New to English readers: yes
- Confidence: high
- Notes: New fact on Louis's finances and the statue's history.
- Extraction ID: J-F181

### F-EW-021 — Portrait of Mère Marie de Gonzague: charm, instability, jealousy
- Claim: Marie Davy de Virville entered on 29 September 1860, aged 26, and became Sr Marie de Gonzague. She was tall, distinguished, with a very pleasant voice, pious and simple. But the memoir calls her "badly balanced": at times too gay, at times in black melancholy over nothing, with strange moods despite robust health. She did extraordinary penances and had "a heart of gold", but an often unconscious jealousy grew with the years and caused clashes and "terrible scenes".
- When / where: 1860–1904
- People: Mère Marie de Gonzague
- Witness: Mère Agnès and the five signers; SAW from 1882
- Source: PA 6, [358], S12 6 Jul 1915
- New to English readers: yes (in this detail)
- Confidence: medium — hostile group document, but by close witnesses
- Notes: She was sub-prioress from 8 July 1866 and prioress from 22 October 1874; the memoir says she held the office 21 years in all. The superior Abbé Cagniard put her in office early "to cure her odd temper" — the memoir calls this "a fatal error".
- Extraction ID: B-F21

### F-EW-027 — Who Marthe was (editors' note)
- Claim: Désirée-Florence-Marthe Cauvin, born 16 July 1865 at Giverville (Eure), lost her parents early and grew up in orphanages in Paris and Bernay. She entered on 23 Dec 1887, took the habit 2 May 1889 and was professed 23 Sept 1890. Her obituary circular calls her of mediocre intelligence, with a spirit of contradiction she never fully mastered, but frank, good-hearted and devoted. Piat speaks of narrowness, brutal frankness and aggressiveness; she was excessively attached to Gonzague, "her servant and follower". She died 4 Sept 1916.
- When / where: 1865–1916
- People: Sr Marthe; Fr Piat
- Witness: editors' note
- Source: PO 15 introduction; PA 18 introduction
- New to English readers: partial
- Confidence: high for dates
- Notes: PA p. 1058: her father Alphonse Cauvin was a shepherd ("berger"). Thérèse wrote the Prayer for humility for her birthday on 16 July 1897. The editors say it was Marthe who, lacking judgement, served Thérèse dried-up leftovers and invited her to warm herself in the kitchen.
- Extraction ID: E-F165

### F-EW-028 — Marie des Anges's early excessive attachment to a prioress
- Claim: As a postulant she became "madly" attached to prioress Mère Marie-Baptiste and fiercely jealous of a fellow novice; she heard inwardly "You make me suffer still more." She told the novice Thérèse about these early weaknesses to warn her against too-human affection.
- When / where: 1866–67; told c. 1888–90

- Claim: Mélanie Lebon, born 9 Sept 1869 at Plouguenast (Brittany), had a poor and hard-working childhood. ### F-EW-462 — Her work assignments, year by year
- Claim: From entry: linen room for nine months; after her clothing, refectory for two years; then sacristy until June 1892. From then to February 1893: painting work (the oratory fresco, altar ornaments, images sold outside). In that period she was also named "tierce" (third companion) of the bursar and went with her whenever workmen came in. At the 1893 elections she was named portress (tourière assistant inside) while still painting. In March 1896 she went back to the sacristy. After she fell really ill she was taken off it and got leave to help a mentally ill sister in the linen room until her strength gave out. She took to bed in the infirmary on 8 July 1897.
- When / where: 1888–1897
- People: Thérèse
- Witness: Mère Agnès
- Source: PA 6, [371]–[372], S12 6 Jul 1915

### F-EW-469 — The night-light for the prioress's relatives: "the devil tempted me to revolt"
- Claim: She was asked to prepare a night-light for Mère de Gonzague's sister and little grand-nephew, who, against custom, often stayed in the outside turn-sisters' building. She told Pauline the devil tempted her violently to revolt, not only against the lamp that wasted her time but against the prioress, who put part of the community at her family's service and allowed her own relatives what she would never allow other sisters' families. She asked God to calm the storm and prepared the lamp as if it were for the Virgin and the Child Jesus, with not a grain of dust. Her heart grew calm, and she was ready to serve the prioress's relatives all night. From that day she resolved never to judge whether orders were useful.

### F-EW-910 — Illness chronology: throat 1894, cough 1896, creosote by the spoon
- Claim: When Céline entered in September 1894, Thérèse was already treated for a very inflamed throat. The illness became alarming only in April 1896. She hid the haemorrhage of Holy Thursday ("the accident of 4 April") and kept the full community life. During 1896 she developed a persistent cough. Treatments: tiring frictions, blistering plasters and cupping glasses, tincture of iodine, and creosote taken pure by the spoonful, not in capsules as later. Céline sees her still going at the set hour for her remedy, never forgetting it because it was unpleasant.
- When / where: 1894–97
- People: Thérèse; Céline
- Witness: Céline, saw it
- Source: PA 8, [781]–[782], Session 37
- New to English readers: yes (treatments)
- Confidence: high; date inconsistency noted
- Notes: Holy Thursday 1896 was 2 April; "4 April" is an error.
- Extraction ID: D-F287

### F-EW-911 — Mother Hermance's notes; chaplains, superior, gardener, doctor, turn sisters
- Claim: Mother Hermance du Cœur de Jésus esteemed her and during her illness passed Céline little notes for her and sent constant verbal messages. The sacristan-gardener said that though she was veiled he recognised her by her grave, religious bearing. Abbé Faucon, replacing the sick chaplain, heard her confession shortly before her death and came out very moved, saying she was "confirmed in grace". Dr de Cornière was edified by her patience and heavenly smile, as were the turn sisters who came in on Sundays to watch her during Mass.

### F-EW-996 — History of the manuscripts, and Gonzague's condition for publication
- Claim: One winter evening early in 1895 Thérèse told stories of her childhood. At Sr Marie du Sacré-Cœur's prompting, Pauline, as prioress, ordered her to write her childhood memories for her sisters only. She wrote in free time and gave the notebook on 20 January 1896. When Mère de Gonzague was prioress again, Pauline persuaded her on 2 June 1897 to order the continuation; it was written in June 1897 at one go without erasures, amid constant interruptions. She stopped writing in early July 1897. The chapter written for Marie in the 1896 retreat is the third piece. After her death Mère de Gonzague agreed to publish the three texts only if they were altered so all seemed addressed to her. In April 1910 Sr Marie du Sacré-Cœur restored the original; an authentic copy went to Rome; the 1914 edition restored the three-part distinction.
- When / where: 1895–1898; 1910; 1914
- People: Thérèse; Mère Agnès; Sr Marie du Sacré-Cœur; Mère Marie de Gonzague
- Witness: Mère Agnès, actor
- Source: PA 6, [500]–[501], S19 15 Jul 1915
- New to English readers: partial (known to specialists; the condition imposed by Gonzague is less known)
- Confidence: high
- Notes: She says the changes "did not change the substance". The 1910 editors' note shows the 1910 court was told of cuts and changes.
- Extraction ID: B-F149

- Claim: Mother Marie de Gonzague, thinking the agony would last longer, sent the community away. Céline calls this a cruel trial for the dying girl, who saw her release delayed. ### F-EW-1683 — Last words and the final gaze: 7:20 p.m.
- Claim: A moment later she felt life leaving her. Looking at her crucifix she said: "Oh!... I love Him!... My God, I... love... you!!!" These were her last words. She sank back on the pillow, head bent to the right; then, as if called by a heavenly voice, she suddenly sat up firmly and fixed a point a little above the statue of Mary, staying so "a long time (a few minutes)", eyes radiant as in ecstasy. She breathed her last at 7:20 p.m. Céline believes they witnessed her judgment: her look showed astonishment and seemed unable to bear the sight of so much love.
- When / where: infirmary, Thursday 30 September 1897, 7:20 p.m.
- People: Thérèse; Céline; Mother Agnès; Sr Marie du Sacré-Cœur; the community (called back)
- Witness: Céline, present
- Source: PA 8, [792], [794]–[795], Session 38
- Original words: « Oh!... je l'aime!... mon Dieu, je... vous... aime!!!... »
- Translation: "Oh!... I love Him!... My God, I... love... you!!!"
- New to English readers: partial
- Confidence: high
- Notes: CONFLICT with Marie: time 7:15 (Marie) vs 7:20 (Céline); Marie says she did not speak from five o'clock; Céline reports speech in the agony. Both agree on the upward gaze of several minutes. See M-EW-031.

### F-EW-1685 — Last words heard by MT on the afternoon of 30 Sept 1897
- Claim: On the day of her death MT came to the infirmary (PO: after Vespers; PA: about 3 pm). The agony was terrible. Thérèse's hands were all purple; she clasped them in anguish and cried out in a voice made clear and strong by pain, calling on God and Mary, saying the cup was full to the brim and she would never know how to die. The prioress said courage, it is almost over. Thérèse said no, it might last months. Asked if she would accept that, she said "Je le veux bien" and her head fell back on the pillow, calm. MT left, unable to bear it.

### F-EW-1692 — The death: MdA's two accounts
- Claim: (1911) In the afternoon of 30 Sept the community gathered; agony began at 4:30. Thérèse thanked the community with a smile, held the crucifix, cold sweat on her face, trembling in all limbs. ### F-EW-2123 — "Comtesse de X": the prioress's sister and the 20,000-franc loan
- Claim: One of her sisters, "the Comtesse de X", had spoiled her only daughter, who dominated her. The countess wrote to the prioress constantly about her troubles; the prioress's mood each day depended on the news, which even became the theme of the novitiate hour. Though rich, the countess lived like a poor woman in secret for fear of her daughter. She borrowed 20,000 francs from the community, stopped paying the interest, and bank notes sent now and then had to be thanked for as gifts. After her death the community got back the 20,000 francs plus 2,000 francs of arrears "asked at random", because the prioress had kept no exact accounts.
- When / where: 1880s–1890s
- People: Mère Marie de Gonzague; her sister (unnamed); the niece
- Witness: memoir
- Source: PA 6, [365]–[366], S12 6 Jul 1915
- New to English readers: yes
- Confidence: medium
- Notes: —
- Extraction ID: B-F38

### F-EW-2124 — The whole community served the countess: embroidery, miniatures, portraits, dressings
- Claim: The countess treated the Carmel as her house. When she came to Lisieux, she used the superior's parlour and a room by the turn, with her grandchildren, and had to be served "like a queen"; the nuns sighed when told she had come. All fancy-work given at the prioress's feasts went to her. Her coat of arms was embroidered free on tablecloths, handkerchiefs and piano covers. For a grandson's First Communion she ordered dozens of parchment images, "real miniatures". The nuns restored old family portraits from her château attic and made two copies of one. In her long illness the Carmel paid her specialist and remedies and supplied dressings, and a lay sister washed the pus-soaked linen after days in the post. They also mended and washed all her linen and stockings.
- When / where: 1880s–1890s
- People: Mère Marie de Gonzague; her sister; an unnamed lay sister
- Witness: memoir
- Source: PA 6, [366]–[367], S12 6 Jul 1915
- New to English readers: yes
- Confidence: medium
- Notes: Thérèse was one of the house painters in these years (F-EW-1082), but the memoir does not say she painted for the countess.
- Extraction ID: B-F39

### F-EW-2125 — Superiors and confessors counselled patience: "They would burn your convent"
- Claim: Some clear-sighted sisters, after suffering in silence, tried to complain. Confessors and superiors, afraid of her influence, advised patience "to keep the peace, so nothing is known outside". Abbé Delatroëtte once said: "They would burn your convent." The prioress also kept the bishop away from house business as much as she could. The nuns felt remorse after trying to shake off her yoke: she had built half the monastery with her collecting and had received almost all of them.

## Added cards — gap fill (batch N, stage 2 continuation)

Numbering continues from F-EW-2447. These cards were appended by hand. They are not date-sorted. Extraction IDs use batch letter N.
W1 = https://archives.carmeldelisieux.fr/naissance-dune-sainte/les-proces-la-sainte-de-therese/le-proces-ordinaire/les-temoignages-du-proces-ordinaire/ (section "Témoin 33"); W2 = the Apostolic Process page (see sources.md).

### F-EW-2448 — Bishop Giannattasio: who he was and how he testified
- Claim: Nicola Giannattasio was born at Bisceglie on 17 Jan 1871 and ordained priest on 21 Dec 1893. He became Bishop of Nardò on 30 Nov 1908 (consecrated 31 Dec 1908). Nardò borders the diocese of Gallipoli. He testified in Italian on 21–22 Aug 1911 (sessions 86–87, f. 1309v–1329v). The promoter of the faith, M. Dubosq, translated his words into French at once. Later he refused the see of Otranto, became titular archbishop of Pessinus, lived in Rome, and died at Frascati on 24 Aug 1959.
- When / where: 21–22 Aug 1911, Bayeux–Lisieux tribunal
- People: Nicola Giannattasio; Dubosq (promoter of the faith)
- Witness: editors' introduction (Carmel site), not the witness himself
- Source: PO 33, introduction and headings [1310v]–[1311r], W1; rights: facts-only
- New to English readers: yes
- Confidence: high
- Notes: The editors also note that he knew Dante, was a friend of the composer Perosi, and published Saggi di apologia cattolica (1916). The court used a French translation, so the French text is not the witness's own wording.
- Extraction ID: N-F01

### F-EW-2449 — He testifies only on Gallipoli, and says his desire is for God's glory
- Claim: The bishop said he came mainly to speak of the "prodigious facts" at the Carmel of Gallipoli (Articles 145, 145a, 145b). He said he knew them by personal knowledge and would name reliable witnesses where he used them. He said he had strong devotion to the Servant of God and wished her cause to succeed "for no human feeling", only for God's glory and the edification of souls in the present time. For questions 10–26 (her life) he said he knew nothing in particular.
- When / where: 21 Aug 1911, session 86
- People: Giannattasio
- Witness: Giannattasio
- Source: PO 33, [1311r]–[1311v], W1
- Original words: « Je sais de science personnelle ce que je rapporterai sur ces faits. »
- Translation: "What I will report on these facts I know by personal knowledge."
- New to English readers: yes
- Confidence: high
- Notes: He never met Thérèse. His evidence covers the cult and the Gallipoli events, and his view of her teaching.
- Extraction ID: N-F02

### F-EW-2450 — "A new way" of holiness: Francis of Assisi, Francis de Sales, Teresa
- Claim: The bishop judged her holiness "among the most eminent in the Church" and "characteristic": in Providence's plan it traces a new way to perfection. Asked what "new" means, he said it is like a man of genius who gives a new way to grasp an unchanging truth. He named St Francis of Assisi, St Francis de Sales and St Teresa as "typical" saints who lit up one virtue of the Gospel by their example, not only their teaching. In his view Thérèse became a "new exemplary cause" of holiness. The one authoritative cause of all holiness stays the same.
- When / where: 21 Aug 1911, session 86
- People: Giannattasio; Francis of Assisi; Francis de Sales; Teresa of Avila
- Witness: Giannattasio (opinion, not eyewitness)
- Source: PO 33, [1311v]–[1312r], W1
- Original words: « une nouvelle cause exemplaire » de sainteté
- Translation: a "new exemplary cause" of holiness
- New to English readers: yes
- Confidence: high
- Notes: Useful for the "connections to other saints" and "what set her apart" scope items. It is a bishop's theological opinion from 1911.
- Extraction ID: N-F03

### F-EW-2451 — Her special way: love of trust and abandonment, and "little acts"
- Claim: Asked what her special way is, the bishop said: love of God seen as love of trust and abandonment, and the practice of "little acts" of the virtues. He saw "heroic" steadiness in these small acts from her early childhood, through her time in the world, to her death at Carmel. In his view this shows that the highest perfection is open to "little souls", and that most souls today are "little souls" in her sense.
- When / where: 21 Aug 1911, session 86
- People: Giannattasio
- Witness: Giannattasio
- Source: PO 33, [1312v], W1
- Original words: « la plus haute perfection est accessible même aux "petites âmes" »

He said he knew this only by studying and meditating on her Life (Histoire d'une âme). He called the Life "a masterpiece" of Christian hagiography and "a wonderful ascetic directory".

### F-EW-2454 — How the bishop heard the Gallipoli story: 6–7 Feb 1910, in the parlour
- Claim: Bishop Gaetano Müller of Gallipoli invited Giannattasio on 6 Feb 1910 to pontificate for St Agatha, patron of Gallipoli. Müller told him of the 16 Jan event a few days after it happened. On 7 Feb 1910 Müller led him to the Carmel parlour and ordered the prioress, Mother Carmela of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, to tell it. She was very reluctant. She told it only under an order of obedience. Giannattasio said her face changed as she spoke and took a "heavenly" look that deeply impressed him.

- Notes: He gives his reading of her reluctance: humility, not doubt of the truth. He calls her "very virtuous and incapable of lying". This is a character reference, not proof.
- Extraction ID: N-F07

### F-EW-2455 — The prioress hesitates to say the word "bilocation"
- Claim: Giannattasio noted that the prioress hesitated much before repeating the word "bilocation". She said it only after Bishop Müller pressed her, ordering her to tell the whole truth. ### F-EW-2456 — Before the event: a Marcelline sister, a novena, and a creditor
- Claim: Shortly before, a Marcelline sister of Milan (from the house at Lecce) had visited the Gallipoli Carmel and said a few words about Sister Thérèse. The bishop added that the creditor had pressed the monastery fiercely for 16 days, asking for payment each day. He said any money at hand would at once have been given to him.

### F-EW-2457 — The apparition's caress and the first guess that it was St Teresa
- Claim: In the account the prioress gave, the visitor put her hand on the prioress's head and set the folds of her veil straight "as a caress". ### F-EW-2458 — The sacristans, the drawer, and "one must not believe in dreams"
- Claim: At Mass that morning the two sacristans saw the prioress was pale and wished to put her to bed and call the doctor. She said, as if mocking them, that one must not believe in dreams. The sisters, moved by a kind of religious fear, dared not open the drawer. The prioress had to open it herself and found the 500 livres.

### F-EW-2459 — Testing the natural explanations (sleepwalking, hidden money, fraud)
- Claim: Asked whether the prioress might have been a sleepwalker or nervous, so that she put money already in the house into the box, the bishop called this "absolutely inadmissible". His reasons: she was of very sound mind, then and later; the monastery was in extreme poverty and the country itself poor, "little religious and little generous", with no benefactor for such sums; the creditor had pressed for 16 days; and Bishop Müller's very severe inquiry found no natural explanation. Giannattasio said Müller would have seized any pretext to end the affair.

### F-EW-2460 — Later sums: the bishop did not verify them and gives them less weight
- Claim: The bishop said that for the events from 16 Jan 1910 to 16 Jan 1911 (surplus in the accounts) he did not give them the same weight, because he had not checked them himself. Müller had put her through "so many trials, examinations and vexations" that she gained nothing by lying. Müller also said the whole community's spiritual progress was extraordinary and coincided with the events; Giannattasio confirmed this from directing their retreats.

### F-EW-2461 — Why he sent 500 livres, and the timing of the Christmas gift
- Claim: The bishop had a special devotion to the Servant of God: he asked her, and had the Carmelites ask her, to help with hard problems in running his diocese. To please her, he thought of giving the Gallipoli Carmel 500 livres, the same sum as in the apparition, on the anniversary date. He hesitated because Gallipoli was not his diocese. On Christmas day 1910 a benefactor gave him 1,000 livres to use as he wished. He said at once: "Sister Thérèse comes to my aid", and hesitated no more.

- People: Giannattasio; unnamed benefactor

### F-EW-2462 — The sealed envelope: how he prepared it (28 Dec 1910)
- Claim: On 28 Dec 1910 a trusted person from Gallipoli visited him. Alone and unseen, he put a 500-livre note into a small open envelope with his visiting card. On the card he wrote "In memoriam... My way is sure, and I was not mistaken in following it" (Sister Thérèse of Lisieux to Sister Maria Carmela, 16 Jan 1910) and "Pray for me every day". He wrote "In memoriam" on the small envelope. He put it in a double "security" envelope (inner blue thin paper, outer stronger and lighter), sealed with wax and his coat of arms. Outside he wrote: to be put in the usual small box and opened by the prioress on 16 Jan 1911. He told the messenger only to take care of it.
- When / where: 28 Dec 1910, Nardò
- People: Giannattasio; an unnamed messenger from Gallipoli
- Witness: Giannattasio
- Source: PO 33, [1319r]–[1319v], W1

- Confidence: high
- Notes: He stresses that the words "In memoriam" could not be read through the double envelope, and that the messenger did not know the contents.
- Extraction ID: N-F15

### F-EW-2463 — 16 Jan 1911: the prioress will not open the envelope
- Claim: On 16 Jan 1911, at about 4 p.m., the bishop went to the Carmel parlour by Müller's order to set the timetable of the eight-day retreat he was to preach. She had written him earlier: "Do not fail to come yourself on the 16th; it seems to me the Servant of God wants to give you a sensible, though indirect, sign of her supernatural action." He thought she wished to avoid new trouble and public attention. A few days before, she had seen that the envelope had grown thicker.

### F-EW-2465 — Opening the envelope: 500 livres in, 300 livres extra found
- Claim: The prioress tore one corner of the strong, well-gummed envelope and opened it with her finger. Then, without touching the contents, she handed it through the grille: "Take it, since it is yours." The bishop saw more notes than the 500 he had put in: two of 100 and two of 50 livres in the second, thin envelope. His small envelope lay in the middle. His first thought was that his 500 note had been changed for smaller notes. The prioress said: count, perhaps this is the 300 the sisters asked for. She offered to call the sisters and have him give the sum "as from himself". One 50-livre note gave off a light smell of roses. ### F-EW-2492 — Mère Isabelle du Sacré-Cœur: who she was (editors' note)
- Claim: Yvonne-Ernestine Daurelle was born at Epinac (Saône-et-Loire) on 29 Jan 1882. She thought of entering a Spanish Carmel of St Teresa, but after reading Histoire d'une âme she entered Lisieux on 13 Jan 1904. She took the habit on 21 Jan 1905 and made profession on 19 Mar 1906. She suffered much from ill health and inner trials. She soon helped at the novitiate, was elected sub-prioress on 27 Nov 1909 (per her own deposition), and then acted as novice mistress. She wrote the Vie abrégée of Thérèse (translated into more than twenty languages), prepared volumes III and IV of Pluie de roses (1913, 1914) and a book on the Carmel's foundation (Bar-le-Duc 1912). She died of phthisis on 31 Jul 1914, after the introduction of the cause (10 Jun 1914).
- When / where: 1882–1914, Epinac / Lisieux
- People: Isabelle (Daurelle); her parents Ferdinand Daurelle and Louise Marie Marguerite Falque
- Witness: editors' introduction; her own answer 2 (parents' names, dates)
- Source: PO 16, introduction and [634v], W1

- Confidence: high
- Notes: The editors say she deposed on 20–21 Feb 1911 "in sessions 52–53"; the session headings on the same page say 62 and 63. Treat the session numbers as unresolved.

The judges, with the promoter's consent, sent the two notaries, Eucher Deslandes and Charles Marie, to check the copies against the originals in the monastery archive. The copies went into the record at f. 652r–1064r. They are in 28 groups (Carmels of France; other orders; lay people; seminarians; priests; then Italy, Belgium, Spain and Malta, Portugal, Germany, Switzerland, Austria-Hungary, Holland, Turkey, Africa, Asia Minor, India, Tonkin-China, Japan, the Americas, Oceania, translations, Carthage, England, British Isles, and nos. 377–379).

### F-EW-2503 — A country-by-country survey of the letters (Belgium to Oceania)
- Claim: Isabelle listed the letters by country. Belgium: "almost as well known as in France"; a report by Fr Robert, Oblate of Mary Immaculate (letter 184). Portugal: fewer letters; the edition by the Jesuit Fr Santanna was granted indulgences by 13 bishops (letters 208–216). Holland: the Engelen community of Our Lady of Lourdes spread images. Constantinople, Africa, India, China, Japan, Canada, the USA, South America, Oceania: letters in ranges. England: the most ardent. Africa: the White Fathers honour her; Fr Bellière, whom she called her spiritual brother, wrote (no. 356); Fr Hugueny OP of the Biblical School in Jerusalem also wrote (no. 302).

- Source: PO 16, [639v]–[642r], W1

### F-EW-2505 — Isabelle's own words on reading the Life in autumn 1901
- Claim: Isabelle read the book in early autumn 1901. She said she was "conquered from the first pages by the purity and simplicity of this soul". She kept the memory of "heavenly hours, full of light, refreshment and peace". She had dreamed of Spain's Carmels; this gave way to a new dream, to be a Carmelite at Lisieux. She thought that after such a saint's passage, Lisieux must be the most fervent convent in the world. She noted every word "as if the Holy Spirit himself had spoken", and felt led to make the Offering to Merciful Love. She entered "despite many obstacles". At Lisieux the "time of spiritual sweetness" had passed, and Thérèse trained her by the way of self-denial.

- People: Isabelle; Thérèse
- Witness: Isabelle
- Source: PO 16, [649r]–[649v], W1

### F-EW-2507 — Conflict: how the Gallipoli-like "reservoir" was told (Isabelle vs Marie-Madeleine)
- Claim: Isabelle tells the kitchen reservoir story as follows. The stove tank holds four and a half jugs. Marie-Madeleine had emptied it. ### F-EW-2523 — Marie des Anges: "I found joy on earth only in suffering — tell the souls" (after Extreme Unction)
- Claim: Marie des Anges said that after Thérèse received the Anointing of the Sick she said: "I have found happiness and joy on earth, but only in suffering, for I suffered much here below; you must tell the souls." ### F-EW-2542 — TSA: her life in dates (circular, 1929)
- Claim: Julia-Marie-Élisa Leroyer was born at Lisieux on 5 Sep 1856, the only child of a devout couple. Her father died on 11 May 1871 in a smallpox epidemic after five days' illness. She entered the Lisieux Carmel on 1 May 1875, aged 18, took the habit in the same year and made profession on 1 May 1877. She was sacristan from 1898 until her death and a councillor from 1902. She was ill in her last years, went to the infirmary in autumn 1919 and died on 22 Jul 1929 about 11:30 p.m. at the age of 72.

### F-EW-2544 — 'For Carmel, never!' — and two days later her vocation
- Claim: At 14, TSA told a priest friend she wished to be religious. He told her to look at several communities in the town and named the Carmel last. She answered at once: 'Oh, for Carmel, never!'. ### F-EW-2545 — TSA's postulancy: cabbage on Sundays, the coffin-like bed, running in the cloister
- Claim: The circular says TSA felt at ease at once: she took the prioress's arm on the way to the choir saying 'Oh how happy I am!'. She disliked her bed because it looked like a coffin, and turned her back on it. Every Sunday the dinner was cabbage, which her stomach rejected, so she stayed without food until evening; she dared not say so for fear of being sent away. One Sunday she saw the infirmarian carry an orange-flower infusion to a patient and offered up the wish. She admitted later that she often ran and even jumped in the cloisters, and had her eyes raised in choir. For her habit retreat she promised to keep her eyes down for three days and did so, so exactly that the prioress had to tell her, before the clothing, 'But Sister, look!' at a statue.

### F-EW-2547 — Youf to Thérèse on her deathbed: 'Do not dwell on these thoughts — it is very dangerous'
- Claim: The circular says the chaplain Abbé Youf led souls firmly and was not always good at comforting them. ### F-EW-2551 — TSA's dream of 8 Jan 1897: 'Sister Thérèse is called — she must be very beautiful'

### F-EW-2558 — Sr Marie-Élisabeth, the extern sister who knew Thérèse: who she was
- Claim: Marie Hamard (Sr Marie-Élisabeth de Sainte-Thérèse) was an extern sister (tourière) of the Lisieux Carmel. Extern sisters did the outside service: receiving visitors and errands in town that enclosed nuns could not do. She was born at Couterne (Orne), the daughter of a weaver; the biography gives 13 Oct 1860 in the text and 1861–1935 in the heading, and the circular gives her age at death as 74 years 4 months. She entered on 7 or 8 July 1890 at age 30, took the habit on 15 Aug 1890 (long black dress, short cape, black veil over a pleated white cap), and made first vows on 15 Oct 1891. There had been no extern sisters at Lisieux since 1889, and the extern house was rebuilt in May 1889 – July 1890. She died on 13 Feb 1935 after a short lung congestion; she had made religious profession under the new statutes on 8 Dec 1933.
- When / where: 1860–1935, Couterne / Lisieux
- People: Marie Hamard (Sr Marie-Élisabeth); Thérèse
- Witness: later Carmel writers (Agnès, 1935; Marie de la Rédemption, biography)

### F-EW-2579 — Marie's last words and the Thérèse statue: 14 April 1905
- Claim: On 14 Apr 1905, Marie entered her agony in the morning. The chaplain visited at 7 a.m. and said he would offer her at the consecration of Mass at 9, as a little host; she said quickly 'And after?' — 'After, that is God's secret.' Her brother-in-law, the doctor (Dr La Néele), knelt at her bed and could speak only through tears; she asked 'Am I going to die soon?... in how long?' A sister brought 'the Virgin of Thérèse' (the statue that smiled): 'How I love her! How beautiful!' She kissed the Child Jesus statue and tried to remove a little flower from her crucifix: 'No withered flowers for Jesus.' Her last words: 'I am not afraid to die! oh what peace!... ### F-EW-2581 — Isidore Guérin: his youth, his degree, and how he came to the Lisieux pharmacy (1866)
- Claim: Isidore Guérin was born on 2 Jan 1841 at the barracks of Saint-Denis-sur-Sarthon (Orne) and grew up at Alençon, the spoiled youngest of three, ten years younger than his sisters Élise (later Sr Marie-Dosithée) and Zélie (Thérèse's mother). He studied at the Brothers' school and the lycée, gave up the medical career his family wanted, and turned to chemistry: a short training at Alençon, several years at the School of Pharmacy in Paris, a residency in the surgical service at Bicêtre, and in May 1866 the diploma of first-class pharmacist. He took over the pharmacy of Pierre Fournet at Lisieux in summer 1866 and married Fournet's second daughter, Céline, on 11 Sep 1866. Piat says he was a handsome, turbulent young man whose faith declined in the Latin Quarter; a family whisper spoke of a fight in which he barely escaped a sword thrust. His Visitandine sister Élise told him, with amused indignation, that he 'drank iniquity like water'.

- People: Isidore Guérin; Céline Fournet; Sr Marie-Dosithée (Élise Guérin); Zélie Guérin

### F-EW-2582 — The Guérin pharmacy on the Place Saint-Pierre: shape, money troubles, the 1873 fire, closure in 1883
- Claim: The pharmacy stood in the shadow of the cathedral tower of Saint-Pierre, at the corner of the Place and the Grande-Rue, with a four-storey classical double front; apothecaries had worked on the site since 1550. Bombing in 1944 destroyed it; Les Buissonnets survived. Isidore loved the trade and was known for probity; he became an expert chemist for the court and a member of the Health Council. He liked to experiment in his second-floor rooms, which became legendary in the family and made the girls shiver because of visceral analyses done there. The start was hard: the till was often empty; the drugstore bought on 16 Jun 1870 caused troubles and burned on 27 Mar 1873; after restoration it was closed on 1 Nov 1883. Louis and Zélie Martin backed the young household with encouragement, advice and, at need, credit.

### F-EW-2584 — Sr Marie-Dosithée's letters to Isidore: 'I go to God as to my Father' (1870s)
- Claim: Piat quotes letters of the Le Mans Visitandine Sr Marie-Dosithée (Isidore's sister) that he says already contain traits of the Little Way: 'I go to God just as I would to my Father, even with much more trust and abandonment'; 'God loves with an extremely tender love those who abandon themselves to him, and a mother does not have as much tenderness for her small child as the Lord has for the abandoned soul'; 'Our Lord wants no galley slaves in his service.' She sent him the Introduction to the Devout Life and the twelve volumes of L'Année sainte de la Visitation. For his 1875 pilgrimage to Lourdes she wrote that one need not be worthy to receive a miracle: 'the most miserable but with most trust' are heard. Her motto for him: 'I will do God's business and he will do mine.' Before dying she wrote a testament: God alone will be your reward; in prosperity keep your taste and household modest; share your abundance with the poor. Piat sums it up as 'spin the thread of little virtues', the line of the Doctor of Geneva.

### F-EW-2586 — 14 Nov 1877: Isidore Guérin brings the five orphans to Lisieux and finds Les Buissonnets
- Claim: After Zélie's death on 28 Aug 1877, Isidore proposed that Louis Martin move to Lisieux so his daughters could have their aunt nearby. ### F-EW-2593 — Isidore Guérin inherits La Musse and sells the pharmacy (Aug–Dec 1888)
- Claim: Auguste David, retired notary of Évreux, a widower without children and rich, chose his second cousins the Fournet children as heirs. Near death at 75 he called Isidore Guérin to his 'sumptuous house of La Musse'; Isidore brought a crucifix, the one thing missing from the decoration, and reconciled the old man with God. David died on 22 Aug 1888 saying: 'Guérin, I owe you my salvation.' As universal legatee Isidore untangled the will: a princely town house at Évreux, a summer residence two leagues away, art furniture, securities and lands, shared amicably with the Maudelonde family with no quarrel. La Musse (a former seigneurial domain of 41 hectares of gardens, woods and parks above the valley of the Iton) was left undivided for both families to use by turns in summer. On 8 Dec 1888 Isidore sold the pharmacy; on 20 Apr 1889 he bought a mansion at 19 rue Paul Banaston in Lisieux, occupying it towards the end of 1889.
- When / where: 22 Aug 1888 – end 1889, Évreux, La Musse, Lisieux
- People: Auguste David; Isidore Guérin; the Maudelonde and Guérin families

### F-EW-2594 — Isidore Guérin as a notable of Lisieux: reading, politics and the family papers
- Claim: Piat says that from 1888 Isidore lived as a 'notable': a member of the Literary Circle since 1869, he read aloud in the evenings to his daughters and nieces Corneille, Racine, Molière and Shakespeare, but not Voltaire. His archivist's instinct made him collect and file the family papers, his 'cahier' being a livre de raison, and to him posterity owes many catalogued letters of Mme Martin and her daughters. He founded (1885, at Louis Martin's urging) the Nocturnal Adoration group; at Corpus Christi he held a cord of the canopy and built a lavish altar, once with a coloured-glass cross inscribed 'The more they insult it, the more it shines'. ### F-EW-2595 — Isidore Guérin's newspaper campaign: Le Normand and Henry Chéron (Oct–Nov 1891)
- Claim: On 23 Oct 1891 the young lawyer Henry Chéron (24), founder of the anticlerical Le Progrès lexovien, attacked Leo XIII in an article on a letter to Mgr Gouthe-Soulard, saying the Pope was 'derailing'. Isidore knew him: in 1884 Chéron had served him for some months as a pharmacy student and had taught Marie the accordion and been heard by little Thérèse; he then played hymns and had brought a colleague back to Easter duty. On 3 Nov 1891 Isidore answered in Le Normand, a paper about to fail for lack of money and writers, signing as 'A Vaticanard who asks that his faith be respected'. His article repeated 'He derails, the one who...' six times in praise of Leo XIII (including his encyclical on workers). He then rescued the paper financially, became its chief editor for six years, refused a duel, and wrote (Piat counts) 74 signed pieces in 1893 alone. He handed the editorial to a successor in early 1896 because of illness, and kept giving advice and money.

### F-EW-2601 — Marie Guérin at La Musse: the squirrel letter and Jeanne's wedding (1 Oct 1890)
- Claim: Piat says Marie did not enjoy the family's new wealth; she fled the society visits when propriety allowed, was a 'sunbeam' at home but reserved with strangers. ### F-EW-2602 — Dr Francis La Néele, Jeanne's husband: who he was
- Claim: Francis La Néele was born on 18 Oct 1858 in Paris where his parents traded; orphaned of his father, he moved with his mother and sister to Venoix near Caen, studied the humanities with the Jesuits, became a first-class pharmacist and then a doctor. He lost his mother in the meantime. Piat calls him a 'good giant of grave manners', a Christian by birth; in 1901 at Lisieux he improvised a speech against the defrocked priest Charbonnel, who was denouncing confession, and answered the cry 'What is your flag?' with 'My ideal is written on my forehead. I am a Catholic'; the success was enough to end the renegade's tour of Normandy. He also saved from a bad death the old servant of M. David, Arsène, by reminding him of his promise not to die 'like a dog'. After marrying Jeanne he opened a medical practice at Caen with a carriage and a coachman; later at Lisieux, living with the widowed Isidore, he was more worldly; the child they wanted never came.
- When / where: 1858–1905, Paris, Caen, Lisieux

### F-EW-2603 — Marie Guérin's spiritual life before Carmel: woods at La Musse, the poor, and Gonzague's favour
- Claim: Each year, in a quiet period, Marie made a retreat at La Musse, going into the woods four times a day for half an hour of prayer; she never missed her monthly retreat, insisting on preparation for death. With Céline and friends she attended weekly sewing meetings to make clothes for the poorest families. Every fortnight she went to the Carmel for half an hour at the parlour. Gonzague had taken her into affection and, Piat says, was open-minded in admitting Thérèse at 15, and equally favourable to Céline and then Marie, an unusual gathering of five members of one family in a community limited by rule to 21 and, by special leave, then 27. Marie also poured out to Agnès and to Thérèse, whom she still called 'the little Queen'. She often wrote to Carmel in secret, because her parents did not favour a tendency to mysticism.

### F-EW-2604 — Thérèse's letters to Marie Guérin, 1889–1890: LT 92, LT 93, LT 109
- Claim: Piat says the correspondence began in banalities and ended in an intense dialogue in which Thérèse's mastery of soul guidance became evident. On 24 Apr 1889 (Louis Martin's illness) Thérèse wrote that after the terrible trial they were 'more sisters than before'. In May 1889 the Guérins, with Léonie and Céline, visited the Paris Exposition (the Revolution's centenary); Marie, lost in the crowd, saw evil everywhere and dared not receive Communion, writing to Thérèse that Paris was 'a real hell'. Thérèse's reply of 30 May 1889 (LT 92): 'You have not committed the shadow of a sin. You must despise all these temptations... Piat says Pius X later expressed wonder at its eucharistic doctrine and this hastened the introduction of the cause. LT 93 (14 Jul 1889): thorns can save a soul. Marie's reply of 23 Jul 1889 shows she had taken the religious name 'Marie du Saint-Sacrement' and made a monastic 'cell' at La Musse. LT 109 (27–29 Jul 1890): 'I know no other means to perfection but love.'

'Yes, always you should deprive yourself. It is good to be gay in recreation, but there is a religious way of being gay. You are sometimes madly gay, you think it pleases the sisters. ### F-EW-2615 — Marie's profession, 25 March 1897: Thérèse's song 'Mes armes' and the two children ransomed
- Claim: After a year of effort, broken by the community retreat of Oct 1896 preached by Père Godefroy Madelaine (Prior of the Premonstratensians of Mondaye), Marie made profession on Thursday 25 Mar 1897 in the chapter room, without the family present. The profession song sung that evening was written by Thérèse herself, expressing what she would have wanted to say to Céline had Sr Marie des Anges not written Céline's profession song. It is 'Mes armes', on the tune of Gounod's 'Chant du départ des missionnaires' for the Rue du Bac Society (Missions Étrangères), a review of poverty, chastity and obedience as the spiritual arms of the Bride of Christ. Marie asked her father to give to the anti-slavery work of Mgr de la Passardière the sum needed to redeem two black children: a boy to be named Joseph-Marie-Isidore and a girl Marie-Céline.

### F-EW-2624 — 12 July 1897: 'a bed of misfortune — one always misses the train'; 'the thief has gone far away'
- Claim: Marie wrote that on 12 Jul Thérèse had been lowered into the infirmary bed of Mother Geneviève, who had also several times wanted and been disappointed of death. ### F-EW-2647 — Mme Guérin's death, 13 Feb 1900, and what she said about Thérèse
- Claim: Piat says Céline Guérin's health failed in 1899; a cure at Royat in July brought only superficial improvement. On 29 Jan 1900 influenza brought her to the gates of death. Two days earlier her son-in-law, Dr La Néele, in a desperate effort, put mustard poultices on her legs; the reaction was atrocious. After a long sleepless night she said: 'I suffered much but my little Thérèse watched over me tenderly. All night I felt her near my bed. Several times she caressed me, which gave me extraordinary courage.' Abbé Ducellier, curé of Saint-Pierre, who gave her the last sacraments, said: 'In twenty-five years as a priest I never saw the last aids of religion received with such angelic piety.' She held her crucifix for hours saying 'Come, my Jesus, come... how happy I am to die!' To the extern sister sent by Gonzague she said: 'I seem to see in you my little Marie and the whole Community helping me.' On 10 Feb she received Viaticum. She asked pardon of all, especially her servants; had brought her dearest relics, 'a cross Thérèse had received for her First Communion, and the profession candle of Sr Marie de l'Eucharistie'; and said 'Lord, I renew my sacrifice, I give you a second time my little Marie... I offer my life for priests, like my little Thérèse.' She died on Tuesday 13 Feb 1900, feast of the Agony of Our Lord, aged nearly 53.
- When / where: Jul 1899 – 13 Feb 1900, Lisieux

### F-EW-2660 — The Guérin family and the Holy Face: cathedral lamp, family prayer, and the Shroud of Turin
- Claim: Piat says Isidore Guérin took part in spreading the devotion to the Holy Face that the Lisieux Carmel later promoted. It arose in him from reading the life of 'the Holy Man of Tours', M. Dupont. He placed the image in the cathedral of Saint-Pierre with a lamp always kept by him, had a moving copy at home, and gathered his family for prayer before the bleeding features of Christ. When the first studies of the Turin Shroud appeared, he took a passion for them, and told his daughter at the parlour of the stir made among scientists by the photographic discoveries of the 1898 exhibition. In 1902 he bought Paul Vignon's book 'Le Linceul du Christ' and lent it to Sr Geneviève (Céline), who then put all her art into painting the Saviour's face. Three years later he had a full-size reproduction of the Shroud sent for his niece, bearing the seal of the Archbishop of Turin and Baron Antonio Mansio, president of the Sacred Art Exhibition. Piat says this was the origin of Céline's pathetic painting of the Holy Face, which drew a cry of admiration from Pius X and spread in millions of copies.

### F-EW-2661 — Isidore Guérin's last years and death: 'Call me, Jesus!' (28 Sept 1909)
- Claim: Piat says Isidore grew gentler in devotion: 'Oh my poor children, it is finished! I can no longer make my Way of the Cross: I weep too much, it makes me ill.' Prematurely old, he could only regret that he could no longer serve the cause by word or pen: 'Jesus knows he is my life and my all, but I weep to be so indifferent to him!... and yet I would like to die for him!' For several years he had a grave liver ailment with acute rheumatism; a violent crisis struck him down. He asked for the sacraments and the Third Order indulgence and received them fully conscious. In his torment he was heard to say: 'Call me, Jesus!', his last words. He died at home, rue Paul Banaston, on Tuesday 28 Sep 1909 at 10.45 a.m., aged 68½. The funeral on Friday 1 Oct filled the great Saint-Pierre cathedral; by his express will he went to the cemetery in the poor man's hearse, and was buried without speeches. La Dépêche de Lisieux (successor of Le Normand) published a long obituary the next day calling him 'the surest of friends, the most discreet of confidants'.

When Thérèse entered on 9 Apr 1888, only two witnesses of the foundation remained: Mother Geneviève (83) and Sr Saint-Joseph (79), who had been totally deaf for several years, so their relations were 'mostly exchanges of smiles'. For her golden jubilee (20 Nov 1889) she asked for 'no High Mass, no sermon, no parlour visits'. She asked, at the end of her life, for no circular; Gonzague respected it.

### F-EW-2665 — Sr Saint-Stanislas and Thérèse in the sacristy (1891–1893): 'slow and little devoted', 'little sister Amen'
- Claim: The biography of Sr Saint-Stanislas says mutual esteem and affection marked her relations with Thérèse, despite contrasts between the tiny old nun of 64 and the tall postulant of 15. Sr Saint-Stanislas's 'heroic devotion' was admired; of Thérèse, the community soon found she was 'slow and little devoted in offices' (reference printed in the text: CJ 13.7.18). A faultless virtue on both sides allowed peaceful work together in the sacristy from 10 Feb 1891 to 20 Feb 1893. Sr Saint-Stanislas sighed a little for 'little Sister Amen' (Thérèse) who spent 'a crazy amount of time' scraping candles and the censer. But she paid tribute: 'I have always seen her practise virtue heroically and have never noticed an imperfection.' (Memoir of 1906).

### F-EW-2666 — Thérèse's last 'pious recreation' for Sr Saint-Stanislas's golden jubilee (8 Feb 1897)
- Claim: The biography says the community celebrated Sr Saint-Stanislas's fifty years of clothing (15 Jan 1896), with verses by Thérèse ('Loved by all our hearts as a gentle gift of Heaven'). For her golden jubilee Thérèse composed her eighth and last 'pious recreation', 'Saint-Stanislas Kostka' (8 Feb 1897), a short play acted by the novices, in which she gives the young Jesuit saint her own feelings: a desire so great he could not be happy in Heaven unless it is realised: to work still for the salvation of souls in Paradise and return to earth to protect holy souls whose long career on earth will complete his own.

### F-EW-2667 — Sr Saint-Stanislas as first infirmarian in Thérèse's illness (April–Sept 1897)
- Claim: At the 1896 elections the posts were swapped: Sr Saint-Stanislas became first infirmarian and Thérèse went back to the sacristy. Thérèse soon fell ill and the old nun looked after her 'little girl' more from spring 1897. In April–May 1897, when blisters and fire-points (cautery) tore her back, Thérèse was moved: 'She dresses the wounds so gently! I see her choose the finest linens and apply them with a hand of velvet' (Circular). She said the infirmarian is 'there watching that you lack nothing. Ah! why do we not do the same for the spiritual illnesses of our sisters' (DE 393). She laughed at the 'snail syrup' (CJ 6.6.6), was moved to tears by a cooling drink brought one feverish evening (DE 785), said her mind was sometimes 'a little paralysed' by the infirmarian's constant activity ('two thousand steps where twenty would do') while she wrote her last manuscript in the chestnut walk (Ms C 17r); and to spare her deaf old nurse she put up with a heap of blankets in August (DE 520). She thanked her with 'smiles and caresses for the slightest service' (CJ 4.9.1).
- When / where: 1896–Sep 1897, Lisieux Carmel infirmary
- People: Sr Saint-Stanislas; Thérèse
- Witness: Carmel biography (modern), citing the Yellow Notebook (CJ) and Derniers Entretiens (DE)
- Source: Biography of Sr Saint-Stanislas, section 'Avec Thérèse (1888–1897)', https://archives.carmeldelisieux.fr/au-carmel-du-temps-de-therese/la-communaute/soeur-stanislas-des-sacres-coeurs/biographie-de-soeur-stanislas-des-sacres-coeurs/; rights: facts-only
- New to English readers: yes
- Confidence: medium-high
- Notes: Cautery (pointes de feu) and blisters in April–May 1897 are also in the doctors' cards. The 'snail syrup' remark and 'two thousand steps' phrase are new to our cards.
- Extraction ID: N-F226

### F-EW-2668 — Diamond jubilee, 8 Feb 1907: Mgr Lemonnier wheels Sr Saint-Stanislas; she gives him Thérèse's photograph
- Claim: On 8 Feb 1907 the bishop, Mgr Lemonnier, himself wheeled the diamond jubilarian Sr Saint-Stanislas, in a small carriage draped in white, under the cloister. ### F-EW-2669 — Sr Marguerite-Marie: mental illness and Thérèse's dream of the luminous cross
- Claim: The biography says Sr Marguerite-Marie made profession on 18 Mar 1875 with Sr Thérèse de Jésus, and received the black veil on 6 Apr. About 1886–1890 (under Gonzague) she showed 'worrying mental troubles', and 'the whole community was sick with it'; she was hospitalised at the Bon Sauveur of Caen, apparently about 1890, returned 'fairly recovered' (Marie des Anges) and was stable for nearly six years. The text notes that Thérèse, who entered in 1888, witnessed these facts, while Louis Martin was himself hospitalised at Caen in 1889–1892. At the end of 1895 she relapsed. On 24 Feb 1896 (Céline's profession day) Sr Geneviève was asked to pray for her healing; Thérèse said no miracle would occur because at that time she had seen her in a dream entering the community room with a luminous cross on her shoulders: all the sisters looked on in wonder at the dazzling light, while everything else seemed dark beside her. Sr Geneviève (NPPO, 1908) and Marie des Anges (NPPA: 'a very long and very luminous cross') both confirm the dream. She was admitted to the Little Sisters of the Poor at Caen in 1922 and died on 12 Jun 1926. Marie des Anges (1915): 'her heavy cross will surely win her great glory in heaven.'
- When / where: 1875–1926, Lisieux and Caen
- People: Sr Marguerite-Marie of the Sacred Heart; Thérèse; Céline (Sr Geneviève); Marie des Anges; Gonzague
- Witness: Carmel biography (modern), citing the nuns' notes préparatoires (NPPO, NPPA)
- Source: Biography of Sr Marguerite-Marie du Sacré-Cœur, https://archives.carmeldelisieux.fr/au-carmel-du-temps-de-therese/la-communaute/sr-marguerite-marie-du-sacre-coeur/biographie-de-soeur-marguerite-marie-du-sacre-coeur/; rights: facts-only
- New to English readers: yes
- Confidence: medium-high
- Notes: A hard part of community life: a sister with mental illness in a small enclosed house that Thérèse also saw. The dream is another 'prophecy' attributed to Thérèse (no cure). Compare the Lisieux Carmel's 'difficult sisters' cards.
- Extraction ID: N-F228
